doc.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Teddy Powell, Woody Herman's call, Sonny Dunham and joining Will Bradley
summary: Pete leaves Teddy Powell's band for the Herd, and recounts joining Dunham and Bradley, pay figures, Barnet, and Freddy Slack.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: Let me ask you about the first Herd, how that came about?

Well I was with the band — Teddy Powell had a band. And it was very similar as the First Herd in style. On that band was Buddy DeFranco on clarinet, and there was Boots Mussulli, and Charlie Ventura was on the band, and different guys, George Handy was writing charts for the band, and Eddie Finkel, the composer was writing charts. And it was pretty outside in a sense. And I joined the band. I remember being with the band about three or four months, and I got a call from two attorneys by the name of Vellum and Goldfarb. They were Woody Herman’s partners. They were the attorneys handling the band, and in fact if I go back and remember, it was a three way split which is pretty good for attorneys. It was 60-40 and Woody was doing all the work I feel. And about joining the band, so I said okay what does it pay, that type of thing. They said well what do you have to have? I said well send me a telegram soon. I think I said something, I didn’t care to leave necessarily, Teddy Powell, because it was a good band and I was very happy. He said well how about $250, which was a lot of money. Because I remember joining Will Bradley-Ray McKinley when I was at Frank Getty’s Meadowbrook with Sonny Dunham — Carlos Gastel, I finally joined the band after playing with it, and I went to Frank Getty’s Meadowbrook and it was because they had two airshots a night on radio. And being there for three months would build the band. The band could go out and get booked very nice and easily then, because people would know them. And during that stint there, I heard that Will Bradley was looking for a trumpet man. And they were

rehearsing at Nola Studios in New York. And I don’t quite remember how I got there on a day off or something, but Ray McKinley or someone knew that I was interested and they said well we’re rehearsing at Nola’s and, when you can. So I went there and I sat in and they says, “The job is yours.” I think I was making about seventy dollars for the week with Sonny Dunham at the caverns or something. And it was a good band Sonny Dunham had, really, Uan Rasey was playing lead then, and he was just a kid himself. So I went to Nolas and sat in with the band, and they said well you’ve got the job if you want it. And I said oh, fantastic. And it was a hot band because it had the Rogers Silverware program, a half hour every week. The band was featured on the Rogers Silverware program. And I says yeah, I’d like to make it. I says I’ll give two weeks notice. So I joined Will Bradley for a guarantee of ninety dollars a week, plus the radio show paid extra, I think it was thirty dollars for the half hour radio show. So that was big time supposedly. And of course after being with Will Bradley, there was Charlie Barnet, which was an episode in itself. I remember playing the theater in Harlem and Dizzy was there on the band, Al Killian, me and a good trumpet player, a short guy, Jimmy Pupa from Pittsburgh, and things like that, and George Soravo was an outside writer. He was writing charts for the band and of course you didn’t have to play a pop tune to be with that band. But it was a good musician’s band. And then I wonder where I went after that. That was right after Will Bradley and before going to Woody. And then in between I came back to the west coast once and Freddy Slack had a band so I hung around Los Angeles for a while and played with Freddy Slack’s band and that type of thing. And then I went back out and joined Woody’s band again.
